title: When does a truck driver need a dangerous goods licence in Australia?
description: When an Australian driver needs a dangerous goods licence, the TLILIC0001 course, the 500 L and 500 kg thresholds, IBC exemptions and NSW EPA licence terms.
shortAnswer: A driver needs a dangerous goods driver licence, and the vehicle a dangerous goods vehicle licence, when it carries dangerous goods in a receptacle over 500 litres or a receptacle holding more than 500 kilograms. In New South Wales the Environment Protection Authority issues 5 year driver licences to applicants who complete TLILIC0001 Course in the transport of dangerous goods by road, pass a medical and lodge within 6 months.
keyTakeaways: The licence trigger is receptacle size, not total load: more than 500 L capacity, or more than 500 kg of dangerous goods in one receptacle. Drums, jerricans and cylinders under those limits never need a licence, whatever the aggregate.
Intermediate bulk containers (IBCs) are exempt if their total capacity on the vehicle is no more than 3,000 L and none is filled or emptied on the vehicle.
In NSW the required course is TLILIC0001 Course in the transport of dangerous goods by road, delivered by an RTO authorized to present it for licensing purposes.
A current dangerous goods driver licence from any state or territory is recognized throughout Australia.
Every other person involved in dangerous goods transport must be trained, instructed and supervised for their task, but the NSW EPA says there is no mandated course for those roles.
jurisdiction: Australia (national ADG Code; New South Wales licensing example)
regulator: NSW Environment Protection Authority (EPA) and SafeWork NSW, joint competent authorities under the Dangerous Goods (Road and Rail Transport) Act 2008 (NSW); the National Transport Commission maintains the Australian Dangerous Goods Code
appliesTo: Drivers of tankers and vehicles carrying dangerous goods in receptacles over 500 L or 500 kg
Prime contractors and operators of dangerous goods vehicles
Consignors, loaders and dispatch staff who prepare dangerous goods for road transport
Fuel, chemical, gas and waste transport businesses operating in or through NSW

sections.heading: Which rules govern dangerous goods transport in Australia?

blocks.text: Road and rail transport of dangerous goods follows a national model. The [Australian Code for the Transport of Dangerous Goods by Road and Rail](https://www.ntc.gov.au/codes-and-guidelines/australian-dangerous-goods-code) (ADG Code), maintained by the National Transport Commission, sets classification, packaging, placarding and segregation rules. Each state and territory then gives it legal force and runs its own licensing.

As at November 2026, edition 7.9 is the current ADG Code. The National Transport Commission states it could be used from October 1, 2024 and became mandatory from October 1, 2025, with some states commencing later. Notably, Chapter 1.3 of the Code, headed Training, is marked "Reserved", with a note that training is addressed by Division 1.3 of the model subordinate instrument. In other words, the Code itself does not set training content; the state regulations and licensing schemes do.

In New South Wales the governing law is the Dangerous Goods (Road and Rail Transport) Act 2008 and the Dangerous Goods (Road and Rail Transport) Regulation 2022. The [NSW EPA](https://www.epa.nsw.gov.au/Your-environment/Dangerous-goods/dangerous-goods-nsw-overview) says the 2022 Regulation commenced on August 19, 2022, replaced the 2014 Regulation, and that the EPA and SafeWork NSW are jointly appointed competent authorities. The EPA regulates road and rail transport; SafeWork NSW regulates the steps before transport, such as classification, packaging and labelling. Class 1 explosives and Class 7 radioactive substances sit under separate Acts.

sections.heading: When is a dangerous goods driver licence required?

blocks.text: Both a dangerous goods driver licence and a dangerous goods vehicle licence are required if the vehicle is carrying any quantity of dangerous goods in a receptacle with a capacity of more than 500 litres, or any receptacle containing more than 500 kilograms of dangerous goods. The [NSW EPA](https://www.epa.nsw.gov.au/Your-environment/Dangerous-goods/licensing-training/driver-licence-dangerous-goods) defines a receptacle as the container in contact with the substance or article.

blocks.text: The battery point matters for energy and logistics businesses moving storage systems. The EPA notes that empty IBCs with residues are judged by capacity, not by what remains in them, and that placard load controls, such as transport documents and emergency information, still apply even when no licence is required.

sections.heading: What training and checks are needed to get the licence in NSW?

blocks.text: The NSW EPA requires the applicant to complete TLILIC0001 Course in the transport of dangerous goods by road with an appropriate registered training organization, and to check that the RTO is authorized to present the course for licensing purposes. The [unit of competency](/glossary/unit-of-competency) alone is not enough if the provider lacks that authorization.

items: Complete TLILIC0001 with an authorized RTO.
Be certified as medically fit to drive by a general practitioner.
Obtain a certified driving history record showing satisfactory driving.
Provide a passport sized photograph and a copy of the vehicle driver licence.
Apply online through eConnect and pay the fee within 6 months of the training and the medical assessment.

blocks.text: Anyone whose driver licence was disqualified, cancelled or suspended in the last 5 years should contact the EPA before starting the course. Licence fees for 2026 to 2027 are listed by the EPA as $66 for a 5 year driver licence application or renewal, and $101 for a 1 year vehicle licence.

sections.heading: How long does the licence last, and is it valid in other states?

blocks.text: The NSW EPA issues the dangerous goods driver licence for 5 years, renewable through eConnect, and the vehicle licence for 1 year. A current dangerous goods driver licence issued by any state or territory is recognized throughout Australia and allows the holder to drive a dangerous goods vehicle in NSW.

The EPA's public pages do not state a retraining requirement at renewal, so the renewal criteria should be confirmed in the licence form or with the EPA's licensing team before a fleet assumes renewal is administrative only. Operators often set their own refresher interval for drivers, because the training duty on the business continues regardless of licence status.

sections.heading: What training do other people in the transport chain need?

blocks.text: Everyone who performs a task in dangerous goods transport must be trained, instructed and supervised for that task. The [NSW EPA licensing and training page](https://www.epa.nsw.gov.au/Your-environment/Dangerous-goods/licensing-training) says those responsible for managing transport must ensure, before anyone transports dangerous goods, that the person is "sufficiently trained to be able to perform the task safely and lawfully", instructed on what is expected, and appropriately supervised. Managers also need training to supervise others.

The EPA adds that "there are no current mandated training courses for this". Businesses may train in house with experienced staff or use a qualified external trainer, but the training should be targeted to their operations and records should be kept. This is the same structure as the general duty described in [the WHS Act duty to provide training](/regulations/whs-act-duty-to-provide-training): an outcome duty with no prescribed course.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry treats the dangerous goods driver licence as an external credential and links it to the product specific knowledge a licence does not cover, such as the segregation rules and emergency procedures for the classes a site actually ships. That gives the unlicensed roles, which have no mandated course, a defined curriculum and assessment points. See how this applies to [energy and resources organizations](/industries/energy-resources).

faqs.q: Does a placard load always need a dangerous goods licence?
faqs.a: No. A placard load is defined by aggregate quantity, while licensing depends on receptacle size. A truck carrying many small packages can be a placard load needing transport documents and emergency information, yet need no driver or vehicle licence because no single receptacle exceeds 500 L or 500 kg.

faqs.q: Is the dangerous goods driver licence the same as a heavy vehicle driver licence?
faqs.a: No. The dangerous goods driver licence is issued by the dangerous goods competent authority, the EPA in NSW, in addition to the ordinary driver licence class needed for the vehicle. The application requires a copy of that vehicle driver licence and a satisfactory driving history.

faqs.q: Does air or sea transport use the same licence?
faqs.a: No. The ADG Code and state licences cover road and rail. Air transport follows the ICAO Technical Instructions and IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations, which have their own training rules, covered on the IATA dangerous goods training page.
